proposal: The Mandate recommends a high-priority assessment of the delays and functionality problems that have held up the VA's new electronic health record, and treats its timely implementation, paced alongside the Defense Department's parallel effort, as central to VA health care innovation over the next 20 years. It describes the rollout as held back by technical delays, safety concerns raised by local staff, and facility infrastructure not yet modernized for the new system.

status_summary: VA has resumed new-site deployments of the Oracle Health system after the April 2023 pause and added sites beyond the plan it inherited. VA's deployment schedule (updated 2026-09-15) lists 17 live sites: the six live before 2026, four Michigan sites (2026-04-11), four Ohio and Kentucky sites (2026-06-06) and three Indiana sites (2026-08-22). It schedules Alaska and Cleveland for 2026-10-24, 26 sites in 2027, and all 170 medical centers by November 2031. GAO testimony of 2026-09-02 says VA has not instituted an independent operational assessment of the system or produced an updated life cycle cost estimate, and no VA-published assessment of the delays and functionality problems was found; VA officials and press accounts describe program changes such as fewer internal committees, a single group working with the vendor, more staff and more training. Nextgov reported in April 2026 a cost estimate of roughly $37 billion given to lawmakers, with Congress making 30 percent of FY2026 funds contingent on performance metrics and deployment data.

timeline.event: Secretary Collins adds nine sites to the 2026 schedule, for 13 in all (the four Michigan sites planned since December 2024 plus nine new ones), and calls the earlier schedule too slow. He says he met Oracle and VA leaders and will hold the vendor accountable weekly. Military Times reports no new formal assessment or review of the program.
VA names the nine additional 2026 sites, in Ohio, Kentucky, Indiana and Alaska, per Healthcare IT News (dated 2025-04-03); VA's news listing dates the announcement 2025-03-31.

Nextgov reports Collins saying VA cut the number of internal committees so one group deals with Oracle, is standardizing the system and training staff, and is aiming for 20 to 25 more facilities in FY2027. The FY2026 budget proposal released 2025-05-02 included roughly $2.2 billion more for the deployment.

GAO testimony to a House Veterans' Affairs subcommittee (GAO-26-108812, published 2025-12-15) summarizes five prior reports: VA plans to restart with four Michigan sites, deploy to nine more in 2026 and reach about 170 sites by 2031; VA had not produced an updated life cycle cost estimate (the latest, a 2022 estimate, was $49.8 billion) or detailed schedule documentation; and VA had not adopted a VA-specific change management strategy or restarted an independent operational assessment. GAO counts 18 recommendations, 2 fully implemented as of December 2025.

Nextgov (April 2026; first of the month used because the article day was not confirmed) reports VA says it restarted by adding staff, streamlining oversight, involving facilities more and fixing hundreds of problems from the original sites. It cites a roughly $37 billion cost estimate given to lawmakers, about $3.4 billion for FY2026 with 30 percent contingent on performance metrics and deployment data, and a $4.2 billion FY2027 proposal.
Four Michigan sites go live: Ann Arbor, Battle Creek, Detroit and Saginaw (VA's news listing dates its announcement 2026-04-13).
Four sites in Ohio and Kentucky go live: Chillicothe, Cincinnati, Cincinnati-Fort Thomas and Dayton.
Three Indiana sites go live: Fort Wayne, Marion and Indianapolis (Roudebush).

GAO testimony to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs (GAO-26-109393, published 2026-09-02, status as of August 2026) says accelerating deployments without addressing past problems risks repeating earlier management challenges, that VA has not instituted an independent operational assessment of the system or provided an updated life cycle cost estimate (as of December 2025), and that VA has deployed to multiple sites without critical or high-severity test findings; GAO counts 4 of its 18 recommendations fully implemented.

VA's deployment schedule, last updated this date, lists 17 live sites, two more go-lives on 2026-10-24 (Alaska and Cleveland), 26 sites across 2027, and deployment at all 170 medical centers by November 2031.

title: Assess VA electronic health record delays and push timely rollout of the new system
uncertainties: The stage rests mainly on VA's own schedule page and news listing; the news listing's page metadata shows an old last-updated date that conflicts with its 2024 to 2026 entries, and the schedule may have changed since its 2026-09-15 update. The Michigan restart was planned in December 2024, before this administration, so only the added sites and management changes are attributable to current decisions. Whether VA ran an internal assessment of delays and functionality problems is unknown; Military Times reported none in March 2025, and none was found since. Pass 5: two GAO testimonies (GAO-26-108812 and GAO-26-109393) were read through a tool summary of the report pages; VA OIG findings on functionality and patient safety were not reviewed. Cost figures conflict across sources (about $10 billion at contract signing in 2018, over $16 billion later, about $37 billion in the April 2026 estimate, and Collins described it as a $10 billion project in March 2025). The Nextgov April 2026 article date (given as 2026-04-01) is approximate. Coordination with the Defense Department, which Nextgov says finished its own rollout in 2024, was not researched further. The progress figure of 35 reflects 17 of about 170 medical centers live plus the scheduled pipeline, and is a judgment. One web search and several Federal Register and VA page fetches were used; a Federal Register query for electronic health record documents from VA returned no deployment documents. Cost figures conflict: GAO says VA had not produced an updated life cycle cost estimate as of December 2025 and cites a 2022 estimate of $49.8 billion, while Nextgov (2026-04) reports a roughly $37 billion estimate given to lawmakers; the two were not reconciled. The 30 percent FY2026 funding condition rests on Nextgov and MeriTalk reporting, not on the appropriations law text, which was not located.
